rashi:a1.1: Your sons are not by purchase: purchase and gift have no place with them; rather, they were born in his own home.
tosafot:a1.1: In brief: [Just as your son is not by purchase or gift…] One may ask: one does not derive what is possible from what is impossible [a son can never be purchased, while an animal can], as Rabbi Akiva says in chapter HaToda (Menaḥot 82a). Tosafot answer: there the derivation of the Passover of later generations from the Passover of Egypt is a binyan av, but here it is a juxtaposition (hekkesh), and Rabbi Akiva concedes to that, as we say in chapter Benot Kutim (Nidda 37b): “the verse juxtaposed them against your will.” They object: in that same passage about the thanks offering, Rabbi Eliezer’s reason is “and you shall perform [this service],” that all the services of this month be equal to it, which is evidently a juxtaposition, and still Rabbi Akiva disagrees; nor can one say Rabbi Akiva rejects that juxtaposition, for in chapter Mi SheHaya Tamei (Pesaḥim 96a) the two Passovers are juxtaposed for several matters. They answer: since that juxtaposition is needed for other matters, one cannot say “against your will” with regard to deriving the possible from the impossible. They ask further: according to Rabbi Aḥadvoi bar Ami (Nidda 37b), who says the passage there follows Rabbi Eliezer, who does derive the possible from the impossible, and who lacks the answer “against your will,” how is our passage explained? Answer: ours too follows Rabbi Eliezer; or else the juxtaposition of nidda was needed for other matters, which is why he did not attribute it to Rabbi Akiva. Tosafot leave a difficulty from “one does not impose a third” in Makkot (5a), where lashes are derived from death, which is the possible from the impossible, through a verbal analogy needed there for several matters. rashi:a2.1: And he objects: But this is written about a firstborn, and you derive animal tithe from it! Moreover, a firstborn is sanctified even when purchased or received as a gift, since it is sacred from the moment it is born.
rashi:a2.2: The verse states “you shall do”: “So you shall do with your oxen.” This you certainly cannot apply to a firstborn, since it is sacred from the womb and needs no “doing” by which a man would consecrate it.
tosafot:a2.1: The verse states “So you shall do”; if it is not needed for a firstborn: It is puzzling, for at the beginning of chapter Ad Kama above (26b) we expound it with regard to a firstborn, as it says: “The verse states ‘So you shall do’: the verse added for you another ‘doing’ with your ox.” One may answer: we expound it with regard to a firstborn because it is written about a firstborn; but since the Merciful One phrased it in the language of “doing,” we also expound it for tithe, since sanctity through “doing” does not apply to a firstborn.
gershom:a1.1: Apply it to animal tithe: which involves a “doing,” in that he brings them into the pen, calls it by the name of tithe, and marks it with red paint.
rashi:a3.1: For a sin offering and a guilt offering: that one may not bring them from a purchased animal or a gift.
gershom:a2.1: Apply it to a sin offering and a guilt offering: which involve a “doing,” in that he consecrates them.
rashi:a3.2: Similar to “your sons”: the verse speaks of a human firstborn; just as a firstborn does not come for a sin, and so on.
gershom:a3.1: This you cannot say, for we require [a case] similar to your son, which does not come for a sin, and these come for a sin.
gershom:a4.1: But say: apply it to a burnt offering and a peace offering, which involve a “doing” and do not come for a sin.
rashi:a4.1: A firstborn is not a vow or a gift offering, but an obligation.
gershom:a5.1: This should not enter your mind: we require [a case] similar to your son, which does not come as a vow or a gift, to exclude the burnt offering and peace offering, which do come as a vow or a gift.
rashi:a5.1: But say: for the burnt offering of appearance, which is an obligation and not for a sin.
rashi:a5.2: A firstborn has no fixed time for its sanctity; rather, when it is born it is sacred.
rashi:a7.1: At the time of doing: at the time when they are fit to be tithed, the verse excluded purchased animals; and in their mothers’ womb is not the time of doing.
gershom:a6.1: Rava said: That of Rabbi Asi [Rabbeinu Gershom’s text reads “Rav Asi”] is not difficult. For the verse states “so you shall do,” that it must not be purchased; and when did the verse exclude a purchased animal? At the time of doing, that is, when it is fit to be sacrificed the prohibition of a purchased animal applies to it. But while they are fetuses, which have no “doing” since they are not fit to be sacrificed, the prohibition of a purchased animal does not apply to them.
tosafot:a8.1: He purchased ten fetuses in their mothers’ womb: this is not precise, since the same applies if they had been born, as they are still lacking time [to be sacrificed]. Alternatively, he said “in their mothers’ womb” so that the ruling holds even according to Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda, who says that an animal whose time has not yet arrived enters the pen to be tithed.
rashi:a9.1: I saw Rabbi Yoḥanan in a dream: last night Rabbi Yoḥanan appeared to me in a dream, and since he appeared to me, I know of myself that today I will say a well-reasoned matter.
rashi:a9.2: Purchase applies to an animal whose time has not yet arrived: if he bought it within seven days of its birth, it no longer enters the pen to be tithed, and all the more so if he bought it grown. Yet an animal whose time has not arrived is not at “the time of doing,” and still the law of a purchased animal applies to it.
gershom:a7.1: The prohibition of a purchased animal applies to one whose time has not yet arrived: if he bought it within seven days, before it is fit to be sacrificed, it never enters the pen to be tithed, even though he bought it not at the time of doing.
rashi:a10.1: And if you say it is a tannaitic source, it is certainly Rabbi Shimon’s: for in his view an animal whose time has not yet arrived is at the time of doing, and therefore purchase applies to it. But with an animal in its mother’s womb he concedes that purchase does not apply to it.
gershom:a8.1: One whose time has not yet arrived enters the pen to be tithed: and we call it the time of doing; therefore the prohibition of a purchased animal applies to it.
gershom:a9.1: So too, one whose time has not arrived is sanctified as tithe before its time and is sacrificed after its time.
rashi:a11.1: And then bought it back from her: if he has nine others besides this one, they are obligated in tithe. If one of the fit animals comes out tenth, well and good; and if the prostitute’s payment comes out tenth, it is eaten by its owners once it has a blemish.
gershom:a10.1: Which is the prostitute’s payment that enters the pen to be tithed, which our mishna includes in “all enter”: for instance, where he gave it to her and then bought it back from her. [A note in the printed text: it appears from our master’s wording that he did not have the Gemara’s reading “But isn’t it disqualified as purchased? It escaped him…”; this requires examination.] It speaks of a gentile prostitute, who is not obligated in tithe, and when he bought it back from her it is as if he bought it not at the time of doing, so the prohibition of a purchased animal does not apply to it; therefore it enters the pen to be tithed. Another version is given: for instance, where he gave her the fetus of his cow and bought it back from her while it was still a fetus, so that the prohibition of a purchased animal does not apply to it. The other version is more reasonable.
rashi:a12.1: It escaped him: this questioner missed what Rabbi Asi said, and so on. And here too it is a case where he gave it to her while it was in its mother’s womb.
rashi:b1.1: Let her tithe it: since he gave it to her in its mother’s womb, it is not disqualified as one given as a gift, and it would be eaten with its blemish if the prostitute’s payment came out tenth. Why would he need to buy it back?
gershom:a11.1: And why do we set it in a case where he bought them back? Let her tithe it, the prostitute herself. And with tithe there is no prohibition of a prostitute’s payment, as we say below: “because their corruption is in them, there is a blemish in them”: wherever a blemish disqualifies, a sexual transgression disqualifies; and a blemish does not disqualify tithe.
gershom:a12.1: We are dealing with a gentile prostitute, who is not subject to tithing.
rashi:b2.1: This teaches us: this baraita teaches that this payment, which was not subject to tithing because the prostitute was a gentile, is called a prostitute’s payment; but had she been a Jewish prostitute, it would not be called a prostitute’s payment, and it would be permitted even for the altar.
tosafot:b3.1: In brief: [A Jewish prostitute: her payment is permitted, and a priest who has intercourse with her is flogged.] One may ask: Rava says in chapter Merubba (Bava Kamma 70b) that the Torah forbade a prostitute’s payment even where a man had intercourse with his own mother, and in Temura a baraita teaches that a prostitute’s payment is only what comes to him through a transgression, but not the payment to his wife who is a nidda. Tosafot answer that Abaye is not speaking of a woman forbidden to the man as a forbidden relation; he speaks specifically of a woman with whom betrothal takes effect, as he gives this as the reason her payment is permitted. And the priest is flogged where she is a convert or a freed maidservant, who counts as a zona; or where she became a zona through another man forbidden to her under karet; or according to the view that an unmarried man who has intercourse with an unmarried woman not for the sake of marriage makes her a zona. As for the implication that a case of a Jewish prostitute who tithes it herself cannot be found: it could be found with a forbidden relation, but the baraita comes to teach that a Jewish prostitute’s payment is permitted. They ask further: according to Rava in the last chapter of Temura (29b), who forbids the payment of both a gentile and a Jewish prostitute, the baraita is difficult. Answer: it was not taught in the school of Rabbi Ḥiyya and Rabbi Oshaya [and is not authoritative]. Alternatively, the case of her tithing it herself could be found, but the baraita teaches purchase in the womb, as Rabbi Yoḥanan holds; though this novelty too would be learned where she tithes it herself, when he gave it to her in its mother’s womb, and it is not exempt as purchased or given as a gift. rashi:b4.1: Regarding forbidden relations it is written “any of these abominations,” and regarding a prostitute’s payment it is written “for it is an abomination to the Lord,” and so on.
gershom:b1.1: “Abomination,” “abomination,” from forbidden relations: it is written here “for it is an abomination to the Lord your God,” and it is written regarding forbidden relations “for whoever shall do any of these abominations.” With that prostitute with whom betrothal does not take effect, as it is written “nor shall you intermarry with them,” her payment is forbidden.
rashi:b5.1: Just as with forbidden relations betrothal does not take effect: for they are those liable to karet, and all agree that betrothal does not take effect with those liable to karet, since a mamzer comes only from those liable to karet, in tractate Yevamot (49a).
tosafot:b5.1: Just as with forbidden relations, with whom betrothal does not take effect: It is puzzling: since we derive from forbidden relations, he should have excluded a gentile prostitute, for we require a case similar to forbidden relations, with whom betrothal does not take effect for him but does take effect for others. That excludes a gentile prostitute, with whom it takes effect neither for him nor for others, as is said in chapter HaḤoletz (Yevamot 45a) according to the view that when a gentile or a slave has intercourse with a Jewish woman the child is fit, for this very reason, that it is not similar to forbidden relations. And Rava himself, who forbids [the payment of] a gentile prostitute in the last chapter of Temura (29b), holds in chapter HaḤoletz (Yevamot 45b) that the child is fit. One may answer: with a gentile prostitute, since betrothal does not take effect with her at all, all the more so is she called a harlot; but with regard to mamzer status, the child is not a mamzer, since she is no more fit for another man than for this one.
rashi:b6.1: Is not his seed: for the child follows the gentile mother, as in chapter 2 of Yevamot (23a): your son from a Jewish woman is called your son, but your son from a gentile woman is not called your son but her son.
gershom:b2.1: And this one is not his seed: as we learn in Yevamot, your son from a Jewish woman is called your son, but your son from a gentile woman is not called your son but her son, as explained there. But this one [the child of a Jewish woman] is his seed, since betrothal takes effect with her.
rashi:b7.1: MISHNA. Brothers who are partners, when they are obligated in the premium: as explained below, where they divided their father’s property and afterward became partners. If they pay a whole sela, that is, their two half-shekels together, each of them must give a small ma’a as a premium, since they are two separate funds, and they are like other people, where one who pays his shekel gives a premium with it. It is a premium to make up the weight; and some say, for the exchange, since two half-sela coins are not changed for a sela without a small fee. Since most people each give half a sela with its premium, when two join and give a whole sela they also give a second premium. These brothers who divided and became partners again are like ordinary partners and are obligated in a second premium.
rashi:b7.2: Exempt from animal tithe: for all the days of their partnership, as taught in the baraita in the Gemara: “shall be yours,” and not that of a partnership.
rashi:b7.3: And when they are obligated in animal tithe: for instance, where they did not divide and the possession of their father’s inherited house still stands, which is not like a partnership, as said in the Gemara: “One might think even if they acquired from the possession of the house; the verse states ‘shall be.’” Evidently they are like their father.
rashi:b7.4: Exempt from the premium: the second premium, if the two of them together give a whole sela, for the property stands in their father’s place. Had their father given a sela for his two sons, he would not have given a premium for the exchange, for that is always the way: one obligated in two half-shekels gives a whole shekel, and it is not like two people who combine their two half-sela coins into a whole sela.
gershom:b3.1: Brothers who are partners: it speaks of brothers who divided their inheritance.
rashi:b8.1: If they acquired from the possession of the house, they are obligated: in animal tithe, as we say in the Gemara. This “acquired” does not mean they bought with money, but that an animal fell to them from their father.
rashi:b8.2: They divided and became partners again: they are like ordinary partners, exempt from animal tithe and obligated in the premium.
gershom:b4.1: And became partners again, that they are obligated in the premium: since they divided, if they gave a shekel together they must add a premium, which is a pundeyon, for that is how two half-shekels are made to outweigh a shekel. Even though they became partners again they are not released from the premium, since once they divided it is two separate funds. And they are exempt from animal tithe because once they divided they are like purchasers, and a purchased animal is exempt from animal tithe. Moreover, since they became partners, they are exempt from the tithe [the printed text reads “firstborn,” corrected to “tithe”], as we say in the Gemara. “They acquired from the possession of the house”: that is, they did not divide their inheritance, and [the animals] grew and gave birth on their own; they are obligated in animal tithe, for the property is obligated in tithe as it was at first, in their father’s lifetime. “But if not”: that they divided and became partners again and then [the animals] gave birth, they are exempt. “They divided and became partners again” is the explanation of the first clause.
rashi:b9.1: GEMARA. “Shall be yours, the males”: “that shall be yours, the males.”
rashi:b9.2: And not that of a partnership: for it implies, what is yours alone you give, and not what is of a partnership.
gershom:b5.1: “All that opens the womb… shall be yours”: the verse states “shall be” to include those who acquired from the possession of the house, that they are obligated.
rashi:b10.1: “And the firstborn of your herd”: plural language; it implies that it is speaking to two, “your herd.”
tosafot:b10.1: For it applies in a partnership: as it is written, “and the firstborn of your herd and of your flock.” At the beginning of our tractate I explained why this verse is needed: one could derive it from the fact that a verse was needed to exclude a partnership with a gentile [which implies that a partnership between Jews is included].
rashi:b11.1: In this and in that: in the premium and in tithe.
rashi:b12.1: That they divided the money: and became partners again, but did not divide the animals. With regard to the premium they are like other partners, and with regard to the animals it is the possession of the house.
gershom:b6.1: Obvious: for so it is, and all of these we could infer from the mishna; what does Rabbi Yirmeya teach us?
rashi:b15.1: They divided the animals and did not divide the money: since this is a leniency, that they are exempt from both, he needed to teach it. It might enter your mind to go stringently and say that they revealed their intent that they stand to divide the property too, and that they should be obligated in the premium.
gershom:b7.1: It might enter your mind, since they divided the animals: for the main effort is with the animals, whose care is great, and each needs to help the other; and they did not care about all this and divided the animals. They certainly revealed their intent that they stand to divide the money, and even though they have not yet divided the money it is as if they had, and they should be obligated in the premium. It teaches us that it is not so; rather, what they divided they divided, and what they did not divide they did not divide.
rashi:b16.1: They taught only: that it is a partnership, exempting them from animal tithe when they became partners again, only where they divided by valuation.
rashi:b16.2: Kids against goats and goats against kids: according to their value. There one cannot say that this is the share that came to him at his father’s death, for certainly at the time of death this one acquired half of the kids and half of the goats, and that one half of the kids and of the goats. So now it is an acquisition, in which one acquires from the other: the young that exist at the time of division are exempt from animal tithe as purchased, and those born afterward are exempt because of the partnership.
gershom:b8.1: They taught only: that when they divided the animals they are exempt from tithe, only where they divided kids against goats, for these are certainly purchased, and it is not a complete division.
rashi:b17.1: But if they divided kids against kids and goats against goats: we say there is retroactive clarification [bereira], and this is the share that came to each one at his father’s death. It is still an inheritance and bears the name of inheritance, and when they became partners again the possession of the house returns as at first, and it is not a partnership. Therefore the young that exist at the time of division are not exempt as purchased, nor are those born afterward exempt because of partnership.
gershom:b9.1: But if they divided this and that equally, they are not purchasers but it is a complete division, and we say of each that it has become clear that this is certainly the share that comes to him; and they are obligated in tithe.
rashi:b18.1: Even if they divided, and so on: there is no retroactive clarification; from the outset they are purchasers, and then partners.
rashi:b19.1: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yoḥanan disagree along the lines of the dispute of Rav Anan and Rav Naḥman.
gershom:b10.1: They divided nine fat ones against ten lean ones: this too is a matter of purchase.
rashi:b21.1: Nine: large ones against ten lesser ones, which is a division by valuation, and one cannot say there is retroactive clarification.
